title: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) updates rules to facilitate E85/E100 flex fuel vehicles
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 OCT 2026 6:38PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has notified amendments to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, to support the adoption of flex fuel vehicles capable of using E85 and other high ethanol fuels. The amendments update the emission certification provisions by expressly including E100 alongside E85. Vehicles certified for these fuels must meet the emission and safety requirements applicable to their category.
E85 is a petrol and ethanol blend containing up to 85 per cent ethanol by volume. The letter E denotes ethanol, while the number indicates its proportion in the fuel.
Flex fuel technology is already used in countries such as Brazil and the United States. These vehicles are specially designed to operate on a range of ethanol and petrol blends using a single fuel tank. Depending on the vehicle's design and certification, this range may extend to E85 or E100, a fuel consisting predominantly of ethanol. Fuel system components and materials are selected for the approved blends, and engine controls automatically adjust operation to the fuel composition. This gives users flexibility to choose fuels within the range certified and declared by the manufacturer.
Greater use of domestically produced ethanol can reduce dependence on imported crude oil. Use of ethanol in suitably designed vehicles can help reduce certain exhaust pollutants and lower greenhouse gas emissions over the fuel's production and use, depending on the feedstock and production process.
E85/E100 is intended only for vehicles specifically designed and certified to use it and will not be applicable to the other vehicles generally available in the market or used till date. A vehicle's compatibility with E10 or E20 alone does not establish suitability for E85. This notification does not require owners of existing vehicles to switch to E85 or modify their vehicles either at present or in the future. Motorists should check the fuel compatibility sticker on their vehicle and follow the manufacturer's guidance in the owner's manual while opting for the fuel choice at the fuel station.
The notification also updates biodiesel-related provisions and makes technical corrections. The rules take effect from the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.

title: Journeys of Lakhpati Didis building Crore-Rupee Enterprises at National SARAS Mela 2026
subtitle: From Self-Help Group (SHGs) to enterprise, at the First National SARAS Mela outside Delhi-NCR
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 OCT 2026 3:40PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Organised as an initiative of the Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India, in collaboration with the Government of Andhra Pradesh, with support from NABARD, NIRDPR and Kudumbashree, National SARAS Mela provides a platform to experience traditional crafts, entrepreneurship and the transformative journeys of women towards financial independence.
Behind every stall at Punnami Ghat is a woman who has believed in her skills, her craft, and herself to live the lakhpati didi dream. Over the days of the Mela, some women from SHGs share what it has felt like to turn a family craft or a first idea into an enterprise. The responsibility of taking charge, the cities that welcomed their work, and the confidence that grew with every step. Some of their annual turnover runs from ₹60 lakh to ₹1 crore.
Walk along the stalls at Punnami Ghat and every counter has a woman behind it, and a story that began far from Vijayawada.
A Lakhpati Didi is a woman from an SHG household with a sustainable annual household income of at least ₹1 lakh, the milestone at the centre of the Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision of six crore Lakhpati Didis by 2029. Under the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM), skills, finance and market access help women build that income. These journeys show what can lie beyond the milestone.
The Lakhpati Didi Experience: Tales of Transformation
Chandrakala, Lotus SHG, Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh: The Craft She Carried Forward
The woodcarving workshop in Chandrakala's family began in 2002, in a household that came from farming. Five years later, in 2007, her husband passed away, and the workshop became hers to run. The early months were about keeping orders moving and keeping the carvers' trust. The craft was all around her. The customers, the accounts and the decisions were new.
Lotus SHG gave her women who understood what she was carrying, and a place to think aloud. Then the work began to travel. Exhibitions and trade fairs took her to Chennai, Mumbai, Vijayawada, Visakhapatnam and Delhi. For a woman from a farming family, every city was a first: a new station, a new stall, a customer who picked up a carving, turned it over in both hands and asked what it cost. She remembers the fair where her stock ran out before the day ended. Today the enterprise reports annual turnover of over ₹1 crore and paying GST of approximately 10 lacs per month and providing employment to 100 + members She is supplying her products through Lepakshi emporium showroom to many other cities. Her products are also being procured from her for gifting to ministers and celebrities.
What she wants next is larger than the number
.
“I want to take this business forward and create work for 500 rural women. That is how I hope to carry this legacy ahead.”
Siddhi, Mahamaya SHG, North Goa: Building a Business Through Social Media
Four years ago, after completing a diploma in Fashion designing, Siddhi began building an ethnic wear business through Instagram, starting on her own. She funded the venture herself. Already active on social media, she saw an opportunity to open a page for her work and reach customers. Mahamaya SHG helped her connect with women who could work with her and guided her on where to seek loans. She describes the relationship as one of mutual support. The group also keeps her informed about workshops on craft skills and marketing, which she and her team attend.
Today she runs a boutique of her own with a team of approximately seven to ten people, including women she has trained herself. She also steps in to do the cutting when needed. Their work includes tailoring, stitching, sourcing materials, packing and helping at exhibitions. She manages marketing through social media and her website
blissbysiddhi.in
, and sends orders received through Instagram to customers overseas through India Post, including Singapore, the UAE and the USA and many more countries. Her business reports annual turnover of ₹60 lakh.
At first, those around her were not very supportive of the idea and wanted her to take a regular job, preferably with the government. Siddhi chose to go ahead with the business. “I wish to help more and more ladies come join my team ,” she says. Over the next few years, she hopes to create work for around 100 more women across Goa and help them become financially independent.
Kunwari Barwa, Mahila Vikas Mandal Baghima Palkot FPO, Gumla, Jharkhand: Building a Ragi Enterprise with Women Farmers
Kunwari Barwa’s journey began with a self-help group in her village, where women started by saving ₹2 each. She encouraged other women to join and took a loan from the pooled savings to buy a cow. Later, bank-linked credit helped her purchase equipment for vegetable cultivation. Growing and selling her produce gave her a way to support her family and pay for her children’s education.
As the groups came together, their work grew. In 2022, they formed a farmer producer organisation (FPO) with 381 members. Kunwari says its membership has since grown to 1,501. The collective helps farmers cultivate ragi, collects and stores the harvest, and makes ragi laddoos, thekua and savoury snacks. From small tables in Gumla, their products have reached fairs in Delhi, Hyderabad and other cities. She puts the collective’s monthly product sales at around ₹6–7 lakh.
The enterprise provides regular work for over 150 women and brings in more workers when orders increase. Fairs have also given the women opportunities to travel. “Some of our women had never even seen a railway line. Now we travel by train and even by plane,” she says.
Singampalli Parwathi W/0 RamiNaidu, Sri Durga Bhavani Farmer Producer Group, Anakapalli (D), Andhra Pradesh: A Small Beginning, a Business of Her Own
In Natavaram village in Andhra Pradesh’s Anakapalli district, Singampalli Parwathi’s family relied on a small farm, two dairy buffaloes and her husband’s daily-wage earnings to make ends meet. While these sources provided some income, they were often insufficient to meet household expenses and unexpected financial needs. In times of difficulty, the family had little choice but to borrow money at high interest rates, adding to their financial burden. Despite these challenges, Parwathi was determined to improve her family’s financial situation by starting a business of her own. However, limited access to capital remained a major obstacle to turning her ambition into reality.
A turning point came in 2018, when Parwathi joined the Sri Durga Bhavani Farmer Producer Group. Through the group, she accessed a loan of ₹20,000, which enabled her to begin buying and selling raw cashew nuts. This initial venture gave her an opportunity to understand the market, build business experience and take her first steps towards becoming an entrepreneur. Encouraged by the potential of the trade, she sought to expand her operations the following year. With a further loan of ₹50,000, she purchased two cutting machines and began processing cashew nuts to extract kernels, which she sold to traders in Tuni. By moving from trading raw cashews to processing them, she took an important step towards adding value to her products and increasing her business potential.
As her enterprise grew, Parwathi recognised the need for greater processing capacity to meet market demand and expand her reach. Financial support from the farmer producer group continued to play an important role in her journey. A loan of ₹2 lakh from the group, combined with ₹3 lakh in bank financing under the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP), helped her establish a larger cashew-processing unit. This investment enabled her to strengthen her operations and develop her business beyond its modest beginnings.
Today, Parwathi processes cashews into 11 different grades, catering to varied customer requirements. She supplies her products to customers across the country and participates in exhibitions to showcase and sell her products, creating opportunities to reach new markets. Her enterprise has grown into a business with an annual turnover of approximately ₹50 lakh—a significant achievement from the small-scale venture she started with an initial loan of ₹20,000.
Parwathi’s journey demonstrates how access to timely credit, collective support and entrepreneurial determination can help rural women build sustainable livelihoods. What began as an effort to supplement her family’s income has evolved into a growing processing enterprise. The business that once seemed difficult to finance now contributes significantly to her family’s financial well-being, reflecting the potential of rural entrepreneurship to create economic opportunities and strengthen household livelihoods.
Behind each of these journeys is a shared pattern: a skill, a group of women who believed in it, and a market that came into view one fair or one order at a time. At the Lakhpati Didi Pavilion, visitors can hear directly from women on this path as they move from skills and collective participation towards enterprise, market access and sustainable income.
Beneath the 16-foot installation “SHAKTI - The Spirit of Lakhpati Didi”, these four women are among the many whose journeys it stands for.
In her address at the inauguration, the Hon’ble President of India, Smt. Droupadi Murmu, encouraged women to build and grow their enterprises further, beyond the Lakhpati milestone. She also pointed to women’s control over their income and assets as a measure of empowerment, alongside their participation in economic activity. She noted that SARAS Melas would be organised every year in different states, giving rural women more opportunities to showcase and sell their products, reach new customers directly and strengthen their financial independence.
The First National SARAS Mela continues till 31 October 2026 at Punnami Ghat, Vijayawada, open daily from 11:00 am to 9:30 pm.

title: TDB-DST signs agreement with Manastu Space for ₹116 crore RDI support to advance indigenous green propulsion technology
subtitle: Project to develop scalable, high-performance and cost-effective propulsion systems for satellites and launch vehicles, advancing technology from TRL-6 to TRL-9
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 OCT 2026 1:46PM by PIB Delhi
content:
In a significant step towards strengthening India’s indigenous space technology capabilities and promoting sustainable access to space, the Technology Development Board (TDB), Department of Science & Technology (DST), Government of India, has signed an agreement with M/s Manastu Space Technologies Private Limited, Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra for financial support of ₹116 crore under the Research Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund.
The project, with a total project cost of ₹277.63 crore, focuses on developing a scalable, integrated green propulsion system for satellites and launch vehicles across the 5 mN to 300 N thrust class. The programme aims to advance the technology from Technology Readiness Level (TRL)-6 to TRL-9, supporting further development, validation and deployment of the propulsion system. The financial support will be provided through Optionally Convertible Debt (OCD).
Manastu Space is developing an indigenous green propulsion system designed to provide a complete propulsion solution for satellites and launch vehicles. The technology uses a hydrogen peroxide-based green propellant with additives, supported by an integrated engine and catalyst system. The system offers improved performance and cost efficiency while reducing the operational challenges associated with conventional propellants.
A key feature of the technology is its scalable architecture, serving propulsion requirements ranging from small satellite applications to higher-thrust systems. The project encompasses the development of propulsion engines and propellant feed systems, including an ultra-high-temperature ceramic catalyst designed for reliable operation under demanding conditions.
The propulsion system has already been demonstrated in space. The programme will build on this technology base through further engineering, system integration, testing and validation, advancing its performance, reliability and readiness for wider deployment across satellite and launch vehicle applications. The project addresses an important requirement in the evolving space economy: propulsion systems that can support more efficient satellite operations while improving the safety and economics of space missions.
The project falls under the Deep Technology sector, with Space Technology as the sub-sector. By supporting indigenous propulsion development, the initiative aims to strengthen domestic capabilities in a critical component of the space value chain and reduce reliance on externally sourced technologies.
Shri Rajesh Kumar Pathak, Secretary, TDB,
said,
“Indigenous propulsion technologies are important for strengthening India’s capabilities across the space value chain. As the country’s space ecosystem continues to expand, there is a growing need for propulsion systems that combine performance, reliability, operational safety and cost efficiency. Through the RDI Fund, TDB is supporting technology-intensive programmes that require sustained investment to progress from advanced development towards deployment. The project with Manastu Space reflects this commitment to advancing indigenous space technologies and enabling more sustainable approaches to access to space.”
Co-Founder & CTO, Manastu Space Technologies Private Limited, said,
“The support from TDB under the RDI Fund will help us advance our green propulsion technology through further development, integration and validation. Our objective is to develop a scalable propulsion platform that combines performance, reliability and cost efficiency while addressing the need for safer and more sustainable propellant systems. This partnership will support our efforts to take the technology towards TRL-9 and strengthen India’s indigenous space propulsion capabilities.”

Referring to the vision articulated by the Hon’ble Prime Minister, he underscored the increasing significance of biology, science and biotechnology in shaping India’s future. Prof. Das also expressed confidence in India’s potential to emerge as a global biotechnology leader and emphasised the importance of translating fundamental research into practical applications. Citing the development of COVID-19 vaccines as an example, he highlighted how fundamental biological research can lead to life-saving innovations and help address major public health challenges.
The curtain raiser event set the stage for discussions on the role of emerging scientific disciplines in advancing India’s research and innovation agenda in the lead-up to ESTIC 2026.

Scheduled for 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, the conclave aims to bring together leading scientists, policymakers, industry leaders, researchers and deep-tech innovators to showcase scientific breakthroughs, foster interdisciplinary collaboration and accelerate the translation of research into impactful technologies.
Covering 12 key thematic areas, including System and Synthetic Biology, advanced manufacturing, energy technologies, artificial intelligence, semiconductors and advanced healthcare, ESTIC 2026 seeks to strengthen India’s science, technology and innovation ecosystem in support of the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
Through its continued commitment to cutting-edge research, scientific collaboration and capacity building, ICGEB New Delhi remains dedicated to advancing biotechnology and strengthening India’s contributions to global science and technology.

The International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB), New Delhi, is a leading centre for research and training in the life sciences. Its research programmes span infectious diseases, vaccines and diagnostics, plant biotechnology, bioenergy, bioinformatics and other emerging areas of biotechnology. Through scientific research, capacity building and international collaboration, ICGEB contributes to advancing biotechnology for human welfare and sustainable development.

title: Sarbananda Sonowal Woos Korean Firms for India's Shipyards, Seeks Global Shipping Rules All Can Follow
subtitle:
Union Minister joins IMO Chief and Ministers from South Korea, Norway and Cyprus at World Maritime Day roundtable

Universal rules, differentiated implementation: Sonowal’s pitch at World Maritime Day roundtable

Sonowal pitches India's growth story to KOMEA members, invites them for a mutually beneficial growth of the maritime sector

Common standards and outcomes, supported by cooperation that enables every Member State to implement them effectively: Sarbananda Sonowal
ministry: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 OCT 2026 7:55PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW), Sarbananda Sonowal, in Busan, South Korea, used a high-level ministerial roundtable on World Maritime Day and talks with South Korea's marine equipment industry to press one case: India wants maritime rules that every country can put into practice, and partners willing to build and grow with India.
Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal
spoke at the government roundtable at the World Maritime Day.
Sonowal shared the stage with International Maritime Organisation (IMO), Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez
;
Nam Jaeheon, South Korea's Vice Minister of Oceans and Fisheries
;
Marianne Sivertsen Næss, Norway's Minister of Fisheries and Ocean Policy
; and
Marina Hadjimanolis, Cyprus' shipping Deputy Minister.
Moon Seong-hyeok, a former South Korean minister of oceans and fisherie
s, chaired the session.
India's starting point, Sonowal said, is that international standards should stay ambitious and universal, while their implementation recognises differences in national circumstances, development, technology and access to finance. He cited the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.
"The objective should therefore be common standards and outcomes, supported by cooperation that enables every Member State to implement them effectively,"
Sonowal
said.
The Union Minister called IMO conventions an "operational lighthouse" for shipping at a time of geopolitical instability, piracy and disruption in the Red Sea, protecting seafarers, trade and supply chains. The best way to narrow gaps, he said, is practical partnership: joint working groups that pair countries that have implemented a convention with countries still building the capacity, training surveyors and inspectors, helping draft laws and setting time-bound plans. The aim, he said, is to leave behind "permanent national capability rather than creating continuing dependence.”
India has done its own groundwork, Sonowal said. Five maritime laws enacted in 2025 took effect in March 2026, India's Maritime Single Window covers 69 ports and terminals, and the Alang-Sosiya yard has 115 ship recycling facilities that comply with the Hong Kong Convention (HKC) within the IMO framework.
The same theme ran through Sonowal's meeting with the Korea Marine Equipment Association, known as KOMEA, a group founded in 1980 that represents 304 equipment makers, design firms, shipbuilders and repairers. Its members include HD Hyundai, Hanwha Ocean and Samsung Heavy Industries.
KOMEA will open its first India office in Mumbai on Oct. 30, a step the two governments welcomed in April under VOYAGES, their framework for cooperation in shipbuilding, shipping and maritime logistics. In February 2025, the association offered to work with Indian yards on design, modernization, technology transfer, joint education programs and the local manufacture of marine equipment and spare parts.
"Every ship built in India needs engines, propulsion, deck machinery, and electrical and navigation systems,"
Sonowal
said. Much of that high-value equipment is imported today, he said, which is the opportunity for Korean suppliers.
KOMEA Chairman Ho-il Kang
said members have begun preparing to enter the Indian market within the next two years. KOMEA members including SB Sunbo, Daeyang, KASEMEC, JO Engineering and others
discussed their
plans for possible investment in India’s maritime sector.
Sonowal made the business case with numbers. India approved a shipbuilding package worth about $7.8 billion in September 2025. Since scheme approval, the shipbuilding output rose 40% in 2025
on a year
on year basis. The output has further grown by more than 80% in 2026.
Since the
scheme approval, the pipeline of vessels receiving direct government assistance covers more than 120 ships worth over $1.27 billion, with export orders making up more than 80% of the value. "We are already building for the world,"
Sonowal
said.
Further, demand from Government entities has also been aggregated by MoPSW to provide
an order
book visibility of more than 400 vessels worth about $23 billion to Indian Shipyards in the next 10 years.
He called the Mumbai office a long-term platform for Korean firms, whether through joint ventures, licensing or their own factories, and said the ministry stands ready to help them set up. The Minister's four
day
visit continues tomorrow with additional meetings and visits.

content:
The ongoing Shilp Samagam Mela (SSM) 2026 in Guwahati continues to attract visitors, offering a vibrant showcase of India's diverse traditional handicrafts, handloom products and indigenous craftsmanship.
A Senior Official in the Ministry said the Mela, which commenced on October 21, is providing artisans from across the country with an opportunity to display and sell their products directly to consumers while promoting entrepreneurship, market access and sustainable livelihood opportunities.
Organised by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Government of India, the eight-day Mela is continuing at Farm Gate, Khanapara, Guwahati, and will continue until October 28, 2026. The Mela remains open to visitors from 11:00 AM to 9:00 PM.
The Official said the Guwahati edition is the second Mela in the Shilp Samagam Series for the financial year 2026–27, following the successful conclusion of the first edition at Dasara Exhibition Grounds in Mysuru, Karnataka, on October 19, 2026.
75 Artisans Showcase Traditional Products
A total of 75 artisans, including 31 women artisans, are participating in the Guwahati Mela, showcasing approximately 40 varieties of handloom and handicraft products. The exhibits reflect India's rich artistic traditions, indigenous skills and regional diversity, with participation from artisans representing the North-Eastern States and other parts of the country.
Visitors are exploring a wide range of colourful and distinctive products, providing participating artisans with opportunities to generate income through direct sales, establish relationships with prospective customers and expand their market reach. The Mela also encourages greater public appreciation of traditional craftsmanship and the skills involved in preserving India's cultural heritage.
Daily cultural programmes featuring local and other artists, including music and dance performances representing the North-Eastern States, are adding to the Mela's appeal. The performances provide visitors with an opportunity to experience the region's cultural traditions alongside the country's diverse handicrafts and handloom products. The cultural programmes are also being livestreamed to extend their reach beyond the physical venue.
Dedicated Ministry Pavilion Highlights Welfare Schemes
A dedicated Ministry Pavilion has been established at the Mela to disseminate information about the welfare, financial assistance and development schemes of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
The pavilion also showcases schemes and programmes implemented by the Ministry's three National Corporations, enabling visitors to learn about the support available to eligible beneficiaries.
LED displays have been installed at the pavilion to continuously screen informational content on the Ministry's schemes and programmes. The initiative aims to improve public awareness of government interventions supporting social and economic empowerment, entrepreneurship and livelihood generation.
By bringing information about welfare schemes directly to visitors, the pavilion complements the Mela's market-oriented activities with greater awareness of the institutional support available to artisans and eligible communities.
Promoting BHARAT-TULIP and Market Linkages
A key focus of Shilp Samagam Mela is the promotion of
BHARAT-TULIP (Traditional Artisans’ Upliftment Livelihood Programme)
, which seeks to facilitate the marketing of products made by artisans belonging to the target groups through physical outlets and e-commerce platforms.
By supporting access to wider markets and digital sales channels, the initiative seeks to expand customer outreach, strengthen market linkages and create additional opportunities for artisans to improve their earnings. It also supports the continued promotion of traditional arts and crafts by connecting artisans and their products with evolving consumer markets.
The Mela provides participating artisans with a dedicated platform to demonstrate their skills, receive direct consumer feedback and explore opportunities for sustained business growth. This approach combines the promotion of traditional craftsmanship with market-oriented interventions to support economic self-reliance.
Advancing Socio-Economic Empowerment
Shilp Samagam Mela is an important initiative of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment to provide marketing support to artisans and beneficiaries associated with its three National Corporations: the National Scheduled Castes Finance and Development Corporation (NSFDC), the National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC), and the National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation (NBCFDC).
Guided by the vision of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi and the principle of
“Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas”
, the initiative promotes the economic empowerment of artisans belonging to Scheduled Castes (SCs), Other Backward Classes (OBCs), Safai Mitras and Denotified Tribes (DNTs).
Alongside providing a platform for the sale of traditional products, the Mela seeks to increase awareness of government welfare and development schemes, strengthen entrepreneurship and facilitate sustainable livelihood opportunities. It brings together market access, public engagement and information dissemination to help artisans convert their traditional skills into viable economic opportunities.
Through initiatives such as Shilp Samagam Mela, the Ministry continues to advance its efforts towards the socio-economic empowerment of eligible communities by enhancing the visibility of their products, encouraging direct interaction between artisans and consumers, and supporting the preservation of India's rich handloom, handicraft and cultural traditions.

title: From Addiction To Independence Karimganj Assam’s Rahul Sharma’s Journey Of Recovery And Rehabilitation
subtitle: NAPDDR Supports Recovery, Livelihood Restoration and Social Reintegration Through Comprehensive De-addiction Services
date:

content:
The National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR) under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, continues to focus on the  prevention, treatment and rehabilitation of individuals affected by the substance dependence.
The journey of Rahul Sharma
(name changed),
a 30-year-old resident of Jalalnagar village in Karimganj district, Assam, highlights how timely intervention, compassionate care and comprehensive rehabilitation can help individuals overcome challenges and work towards a healthier and more independent life.
Following the death of his father, Rahul had to leave school at an early age to take on family responsibilities. Financial difficulties, emotional distress and limited opportunities gradually affected his well-being. In search of temporary relief, he began using drugs in the company of peers, eventually developing substance dependence.
This affected his health, work productivity and relationships with family members. Financial strain, social stigma and limited access to nearby rehabilitation services further compounded his difficulties. Despite these challenges, Rahul aspired to rebuild his life and fulfil his dream of establishing his own transportation business.
A turning point came when Rahul received support under the NAPDDR through the Drug De-addiction and Rehabilitation Centre (DDAC) operated by WODWICHEE in Karimganj, Assam. With guidance from doctors, counsellors and centre staff, he underwent residential rehabilitation and received medical treatment, individual and group counselling, family counselling, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), 12-Step Therapy, yoga and meditation.
These comprehensive services supported his recovery, helped him develop healthier habits and enabled him to regain confidence. Family counselling and community reintegration support further assisted him in rebuilding relationships and preparing for a more stable future.
With sustained support and determination, Rahul gradually regained control over his life and redirected his efforts towards productive work. Today, he operates his own small transportation business and earns more than he did previously. The improvement in his income has strengthened his financial stability and enabled him to contribute more effectively to his family’s well-being. His journey demonstrates how access to treatment, rehabilitation and continued support can help individuals overcome substance dependence and pursue their aspirations with renewed confidence.
The support provided to Rahul reflects the importance of comprehensive rehabilitation in addressing not only substance dependence but also the social and economic challenges associated with it. Through initiatives under NAPDDR, the Ministry seeks to strengthen access to de-addiction services, promote recovery and facilitate the social reintegration of individuals affected by substance use. Rahul’s experience underscores how appropriate care and sustained support can help individuals rebuild their lives, restore their livelihoods and move towards a more secure future.
The Ministry continues to encourage awareness, early intervention, access to treatment and community-based support to address substance dependence and promote a healthier, more inclusive society.

title: National Overseas Scholarship: Yukti’s (Name Changed) Journey from Barriers to Global Opportunities
date:

content:
For many aspiring students, access to quality higher education is a stepping stone towards a brighter future. However, for students from disadvantaged backgrounds, social discrimination and financial constraints can create significant barriers to academic and professional advancement. The journey of Ms. Yukti, a 26-year-old postgraduate belonging to the Scheduled Caste (SC) community, highlights how targeted government support can help transform educational aspirations into opportunities.
From an early age, Yukti faced caste-based discrimination and social exclusion. Her family also experienced persistent financial difficulties, as her father was the sole earning member and worked in a low-paying job. Despite his education, occupational barriers and social bias limited his career progression, leaving the family with limited resources. Yukti’s parents nevertheless prioritised her education and encouraged her to pursue her ambitions. With no financial safety net, she relied on government schools and public scholarships to continue her studies.
Yukti aspired to pursue advanced higher education and build a meaningful career connected with research and academic development. However, the substantial cost of postgraduate education abroad appeared to be a major obstacle. A significant turning point came when she received support under the National Overseas Scholarship (NOS) Scheme of the Government of India during 2023–2024. The scholarship covered her tuition fees and provided an annual maintenance allowance of £9,900, helping her access international education that would otherwise have been financially out of reach.
The scholarship substantially eased the financial burden on Yukti and her family and enabled her to focus on her studies and professional development. Although rising living costs abroad meant that managing expenses remained challenging, the assistance provided essential support throughout her educational journey. Selection for the scholarship also gave Yukti a significant boost in confidence, affirmed her academic potential and strengthened her belief that she belonged in a competitive international academic environment.
Through her overseas education, Yukti gained valuable international exposure and advanced academic knowledge that strengthened her professional prospects. She has since transitioned into the private sector in India, securing professional opportunities and moving towards greater economic independence. While no specific change in income has been reported, her educational achievements and entry into professional employment mark meaningful progress towards her aspirations.
Yukti’s journey demonstrates the role of the National Overseas Scholarship Scheme in promoting educational inclusion and enabling students from Scheduled Caste communities to pursue higher education abroad. By providing financial assistance for tuition and maintenance, the scheme helps deserving students overcome economic barriers, broaden their horizons and build pathways towards professional growth. Her experience reflects how government support, family encouragement and personal determination can combine to turn educational aspirations into tangible opportunities.

title: ASUSE 2027–28 to Align with the Financial Year (April–March)
subtitle: New Policy-Focused Questions to Address Emerging Data Needs
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 OCT 2026 4:00PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Enhanced Stakeholder Responsiveness
Snapshot:
ASUSE 2027-28 is proposed to be conducted from April 2027 to March 2028, aligning the survey period with the financial year.
The survey will feature new policy focussed questions for better understanding of the unincorporated sector.
Gender-specific constraints faced by female entrepreneurs to be captured for the first time.
New question added for better understanding the investment trajectory of establishments.
Accommodating requirements of stakeholder Ministries and other data users in the survey to ensure that the ASUSE framework remains relevant, accurate, and responsive to the dynamic structure of the unincorporated sector.
Following the approach adopted in the previous surveys, the sample design for ASUSE 2027-28 has provision for the generation of district-level estimates by the participating States.
The unincorporated non-agricultural sector constitutes an important segment of the Indian economy. It contributes significantly to employment and gross value added, provides livelihoods to a large number of people and supports economic activity through its linkages with the incorporated sector. Enterprises in this segment operate across a wide range of activities and vary considerably in their scale, organisational structure and operating conditions. Reliable and timely information on their operational characteristics and economic activities is therefore essential for understanding the structure and performance of the sector and for formulating policies that respond to its diverse requirements.
The National Statistics Office (NSO), Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), has been conducting the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) since 2021–22 to generate comprehensive statistical information on this important segment of the economy. The survey provides information on the characteristics and economic operations of unincorporated establishments and contributes to the availability of data for economic analysis, policy formulation and national accounting purposes.
The development of ASUSE has been guided by regular engagement with stakeholders and an assessment of emerging data requirements. The Ministry has undertaken several initiatives in this regard, including the organisation of Data User Conferences, regular consultations with stakeholder Ministries and deliberations with expert groups on various technical aspects of the survey.
During the ongoing ASUSE 2026, suggestions and data requirements have also been received from stakeholders through different forums. These inputs, together with NSO’s internal assessment of the survey requirements, have led to the proposed changes in the schedule for ASUSE 2027–28.
The proposed changes seek to improve the policy relevance of the survey while retaining its role as a key source of official statistics on the unincorporated non-agricultural sector.
Key changes proposed in ASUSE 2027–28
For the first time, questions will be introduced to capture gender-specific constraints faced by female entrepreneurs in operating and managing their establishments. These questions aim to improve the availability of information on the challenges women entrepreneurs face in the unincorporated sector.
Such information can support a better understanding of the constraints faced by female-led enterprises and provide a useful evidence-base for examining the factors affecting their business operations. It will also broaden the scope of information available from ASUSE for analysing the challenges of female entrepreneurs and for informing policy discussions relating to women's participation in economic activity.
Additional questions will be included to capture the different sources of electricity used by establishments. This will provide a more comprehensive picture of the energy-use patterns of enterprises in the unincorporated sector. Information on electricity sources can help data users better understand the energy arrangements under which establishments operate and facilitate analysis of the operating environment of enterprises across different activities. The addition of these questions will strengthen the range of information available from ASUSE on the operational characteristics of establishments.
A new question will be introduced to capture investment in fixed assets over a longer reference period than that covered in the existing schedule. This change is intended to provide a broader perspective on the investment trajectory of establishments. Information covering a longer period can help in examining investment activity beyond the period captured by the existing question and can provide additional insights into the investment behaviour and business outlook of establishments. It will also enhance the analytical utility of ASUSE data for understanding investment patterns in the unincorporated sector.
The handloom and handicraft sector sits at the intersection of India’s unincorporated economy and traditional knowledge systems and availability of precise, granular and actionable data is indispensable for evidence-based policy making for this sector.  In this context, at the request of the Ministry of Textiles, two questions will be included to identify handloom, power-loom and handicraft establishments. The proposed questions are intended to facilitate the identification of establishments engaged in these activities within the survey framework.
The availability of such information will improve the scope for analysing these segments of the unincorporated sector and help address the specific information requirements of the concerned stakeholder Ministry. Taken together, these changes are intended to enhance the policy orientation of ASUSE and improve its responsiveness to the information needs of different Ministries and other data users.
In an important change to the survey calendar, the survey period for ASUSE is being shifted from the calendar year (January–December) to the financial year (April–March). Accordingly, ASUSE 2027–28 is proposed to be conducted from April 2027 to March 2028. The change is intended to align the reference period of the survey with the financial year, as is done in other enterprise surveys like Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Annual Survey of Incorporated Services Sector Enterprises (ASISSE), etc. and enhance the utility of ASUSE data for National Accounts purposes. Financial-year alignment is expected to facilitate the use of survey information in conjunction with other economic statistics compiled on a financial-year basis.
The transition has been planned ensuring continuity in the generation of quarterly estimates. To avoid a break in the quarterly estimates for January–March 2027, the survey will also be conducted during this quarter using the existing ASUSE 2026 schedule. Thereafter, the new survey cycle will commence in April 2027 under ASUSE 2027–28. This arrangement is intended to facilitate the transition to the revised survey calendar while preserving continuity in the quarterly statistical series.
The initiatives introduced in earlier rounds of ASUSE to strengthen the quality, coverage and usefulness of the survey will continue in ASUSE 2027–28.
These include the revamped sampling design, which provides for the generation of district-level estimates by participating States; the use of globally accepted classifications; and the deployment of agile Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI)-based systems for data collection and a more policy-oriented ICT block with questions covering presence of the establishment in e-commerce market place and use of digital payment instruments such as UPI (including BHIM), mobile wallets and POS devices. These measures support the systematic collection of information and strengthen the analytical usefulness of the resulting data.
The survey will also continue to incorporate stakeholder-driven information requirements, wherever appropriate, and to disseminate findings through the Quarterly Bulletin of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (QBUSE). The continued publication of quarterly estimates will support the availability of timely information on developments in the unincorporated sector.
The detailed establishment schedule for ASUSE 2027–28 is placed on the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)’s official website to invite comments and suggestions from policymakers, stakeholder Ministries, researchers, data users and other interested stakeholders.
Comments and suggestions on the proposed schedule may be sent in the prescribed format to nssocpd.coord@mospi.gov.in and tc.dpd@mospi.gov.in by 15th November 2026. The draft questionnaire and the prescribed feedback format can be accessed through the link provided on the MoSPI website at https://www.mospi.gov.in.
The feedback received from stakeholders will help the Ministry assess the proposed information requirements and further enhance the relevance, comprehensiveness and policy utility of ASUSE 2027–28.

content:
Mera Yuva Bharat (MY Bharat), under the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, organised a series of activities during the sixth week of the
100 Weeks Campaign under the “Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat” Abhiyan
, mobilising 2,11,139 youth and citizens across 36 States and Union Territories through 694 programmes, as per the provisional report. The activities centred on
Nashe Ke Ravan Ka Dahan/Nasha Rupi Mahishasur Ka Vadh
, traditional sports, and
Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Par Paricharcha
(Neighbourhood Youth Parliament), combining cultural engagement, physical activity and community dialogue to strengthen awareness about substance abuse.
The campaign used culturally rooted initiatives such as symbolic Ravan Dahan and Mahishasur Vadh to convey the message of overcoming addiction and rejecting substance abuse. Traditional sports activities encouraged physical fitness, healthy lifestyles and community participation, while Neighbourhood Youth Parliament sessions provided a platform for young people and community members to discuss the harmful effects of substance abuse, prevention strategies and the role of youth in building a drug-free society.
The programmes were organised in collaboration with FIT India and partner organisations, including Brahma Kumaris, Heartfulness, FICCI, CIPU, ASSOCHAM and Project Point. The collaborative approach brought together youth networks, community institutions and partner organisations to extend the campaign’s outreach and encourage collective action against substance abuse.
The campaign recorded
2,11,139 pledges
towards the objective of a drug-free India. The activities sought to translate awareness into individual commitment and community-level action by encouraging young people to adopt healthy, substance-free lifestyles and motivate others to stay away from addictive substances.
Through the 100 Weeks Campaign, MY Bharat continues to engage young people and communities through awareness programmes, participatory activities and youth-led initiatives. The sixth week’s focus on cultural traditions, sports and structured dialogue underscores the importance of sustained community engagement in preventing substance abuse and promoting informed choices among young people.
The initiative supports the broader vision of
Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat
, encouraging young citizens to contribute to the creation of healthier communities and a developed India..

content:
Immersive technologies are expanding across India’s education, industry and creative sectors. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting is promoting the Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming, Comics and Extended Reality (AVGC-XR) ecosystem through initiatives such as the
Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT)
in Mumbai. Established as a National Centre of Excellence, IICT collaborates with global technology companies, including Google, Meta, Adobe and Netflix, to strengthen creative education, skills and innovation. Further supporting this ecosystem, the
Union Budget 2026–27 allocated
₹
250 crore
for AVGC Content Creator Labs in 15,000 secondary schools and 500 colleges across India.
From Digital to Immersive: India's Next Leap
Over the last decade, India has built a strong digital ecosystem that has transformed everyday interactions with technology. Platforms such as
UPI, Aadhaar, DigiLocker, UMANG and BHASHINI
have expanded access to services and information. As digital platforms become more widespread, the next opportunity is to make these interactions more
interactive, visual and experiential
. Rapid advances in Artificial Intelligence, high-speed connectivity and computing are enabling this shift from simply accessing digital services to experiencing them.
Click to Read More: India’s Digital Public Infrastructure
and
Transforming India with AI
This emerging phase is being shaped by
immersive technologies
, which bring digital content closer to the way people experience the physical world.
Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, Mixed Reality and 360-degree experiences
can create interactive environments and enable users to engage with digital content in new ways. These capabilities can transform education through virtual simulations, healthcare through immersive training, and tourism through virtual exploration. They can also create more engaging experiences across
culture, gaming, entertainment, retail and other sectors
. In doing so, immersive technologies can expand the impact of India’s existing digital ecosystem beyond conventional screen-based interactions.
The scale of this opportunity is reflected in India’s rapidly growing immersive technology market. The market generated
USD 1,259.5 million in revenue in 2023
and is projected to reach
USD 7,818.7 million by 2030
, growing at a
CAGR of 29.8 per cent
. India is projected to be the
fastest-growing regional market in Asia Pacific
, supported by its digital ecosystem, expanding middle class and rising e-commerce adoption. This growth presents an opportunity for India to move beyond being a large market and emerge as a
global hub for immersive technology
. Building capabilities in research, startups, talent, content and indigenous technologies can help India shape the next generation of immersive experiences and strengthen its position in the global digital economy.
Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies
ESTIC-2026, the second edition of India’s Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave, will be held from 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. The event will be organised under the theme
“Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies.”
Organised by the Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR), ESTIC-2026 will bring together ministries, researchers, innovators, industry leaders, deep-tech start-ups and global experts to advance emerging science and technology. The conclave will feature 12 thematic areas, including
Immersive Tech: Generative XR and Spatial Computing
. The event will feature plenary sessions, technical discussions and exhibitions.

Understanding Immersive Technologies
Immersive technologies are an emerging suite of technologies that create interactive, engaging and realistic digital experiences. Immersive technologies can combine the
physical and digital worlds
. They enable users to interact with digital content in ways that feel more natural and experiential. Users can interact with digital objects and respond to simulated situations. Unlike conventional digital media, these technologies can engage multiple senses and create a stronger sense of presence. For example, a student can explore a virtual laboratory instead of only viewing diagrams on a screen. Similarly, a tourist can virtually explore a heritage site before visiting it physically. The three most common forms of immersive technology are Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), and Mixed Reality (MR). Collectively, these technologies are often referred to as Extended Reality (XR).
Extended Reality (XR)
Extended Reality (XR) refers to technologies that combine real and digital environments through computer systems and wearable devices. It creates different levels of interaction between people and digital content. XR includes Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR) and Mixed Reality (MR).
Virtual Reality (VR)
creates a completely digital environment that surrounds the user. It mainly engages sight and sound to create a strong sense of presence. Users can explore and interact with this simulated environment using specialised devices.
Augmented Reality (AR)
adds digital information to the user’s existing physical surroundings. It can engage sight and sound, while keeping the real-world environment visible. For example, AR can display directions, information or digital objects over the physical world.
Mixed Reality (MR)
combines the physical and digital worlds in an interactive environment. It can engage sight and sound, while allowing digital objects to interact with physical surroundings. Users can see and interact with digital objects as if they were part of the real environment.
Other related tech, such as
360-degree video
and
Haptic Technology
, also form part of the wider immersive technology ecosystem. 360-degree video allows users to view a scene in every direction. Users can change their viewing direction and explore different parts of the recorded environment. Haptic Technology uses vibrations, pressure or other physical sensations to provide touch-based feedback. It can make digital interactions feel more realistic by simulating physical sensations during virtual or interactive experiences.
Stepping Into the Experience: How India Is Using Immersive Technology
Education
Researchers at
IIT Madras are developing AR/VR-enabled learning solutions for rural schools
. The initiative uses digital technologies to improve teaching and learning for secondary school students. It aims to create
immersive, VR-based learning environments
where students can explore subjects such as history, social science, science and languages through interactive experiences.
These technologies can make classroom learning more engaging. For example, an AR-based mobile application could bring 500 years of Indian history to life through animated photographs, interactive maps and archival documents. Similarly, VR simulations could allow students to explore the solar system or study the human body through three-dimensional models. By making abstract concepts easier to visualise and understand, these approaches can enrich learning and help students prepare for higher education.
Heritage and Tourism
The Government is using
Extended Reality (XR)
and other digital technologies to make India’s cultural heritage more accessible and engaging. The Ministry of Culture has adopted digital tools to improve visitor experiences and preserve information about museum collections. One such tool is
JATAN software
, which helps digitise museum artefacts and their records. So far, eight national-level museums and two Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) museums have been digitised using JATAN. Their collections are accessible through the
Museums of India
digital repository, enabling people to explore India’s heritage online.
Building on this digital foundation, museums are also introducing interactive experiences for visitors. The Indian Museum in Kolkata has introduced AI-based interactive features and AR tools to enrich gallery visits. It has also collaborated with Google Arts & Culture on a virtual exhibition showcasing cultural heritage through digital technology. Similarly, ASI museums at Hampi in Karnataka and Nalanda in Bihar offer mobile-based virtual tours of their collections. These initiatives help visitors explore artefacts digitally, making cultural experiences more engaging and accessible beyond the museum premises.

Governance and Infrastructure
Immersive technologies are also shaping how India plans and manages its infrastructure. The Department of Telecommunications launched the "
Sangam: Digital Twin
" initiative, combining digital twin technology with 5G, IoT, and AI for better infrastructure planning. Digital twin mapping is already supporting city planning, as seen in the
Varanasi Urban 3D Spatial Planning project
. By 2035, India aims to build a
National Digital Twin
for major urban centres, creating digital replicas to improve city planning and management.
What is Digital Twin?
A digital twin is a virtual model of a real-world object, system or place. It uses data from the real world to represent conditions and behaviour, helping users monitor situations and test possible changes digitally. For example, a digital twin of a machine can help identify potential faults, while a city model can help planners assess the likely impact of infrastructure projects before implementation. One example is the Mobility Digital Twin showcased by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) at India Mobile Congress 2025. It uses telecom-derived mobility data to analyse how people travel and move through different areas. Demonstrations in Vasant Kunj and Central Vista in Delhi examined commuting patterns and helped assess metro station catchment areas. In Ayodhya, mobility data was used to study tourist flows, travel modes and stay patterns. These insights can help authorities plan transport links, improve tourism infrastructure and make better-informed decisions before finalising projects.
Creative Economy and Entertainment
Immersive technology is a growing part of India's media and entertainment sector, closely tied to the AVGC-XR framework. India's gaming sector is projected to grow from
$3.8 billion in 2024 to $9.2 billion by FY29, according to an independent report
, reflecting the scale of this emerging economy. National platforms such as the WAVES summit are further showcasing India's creative and immersive media capabilities to a global audience.
Powering Immersive Technology: India's Key Initiatives
Immersive technology is supported through the Government's broader
AVGC-XR framework
. This framework covers Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming, Comics, and Extended Reality. India's policy support for immersive technology comes as part of the larger, unified push, not as a standalone scheme.
Click to Read More: Powering the AVGC-XR Revolution
AVGC-XR Promotion Task Force
The
AVGC Promotion Task Force
was constituted by the
Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (MIB)
in
April 2022
.
It brings together representatives from the
Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming and Comics (AVGC) industry, academia and Government
. The Task Force provides a platform for coordinated efforts to strengthen the sector’s growth and development. Its mandate is guided by three key principles. These include
public-private collaboration, inter-ministerial convergence and an integrated approach to sectoral development
.
Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT)
On the Task Force's recommendation, the Government set up
a National Centre of Excellence (NCoE) t
o build skilled talent for the AVGC-XR sector. This took shape as the
Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT),
established in 2025. As of March 2026, IICT has introduced 18 courses across various domains of the AVGC-XR sector, with over 135 students enrolled.
GENESIS (Gen-Next Support for Innovative Startups)
To boost the startup ecosystem in Tier-II and Tier-III cities, MeitY approved the GENESIS Scheme. Launched in 2022, it aims to support around 1,600 tech startups over five years. This includes startups working in immersive technologies like AR, VR, and spatial computing. Through the MeitY Startup Hub, the scheme currently supports
84 AR/VR startups
. It also backs
106 incubators
across the country.
AVGC Content Creator Labs
Under the
Union Budget 2026–27
, the Government allocated
₹
250 crore
to establish Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming and Comics (AVGC) Content Creator Labs in
15,000 secondary schools and 500 colleges
. The Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT), Mumbai, will serve as the nodal agency for planning, coordinating and implementing the initiative. These labs aim to equip students with practical skills in animation, visual effects, gaming and digital content creation. They will provide opportunities to develop creative ideas and gain hands-on experience using industry-relevant tools and technologies. The initiative seeks to nurture young talent and prepare students for emerging careers in India’s growing creative economy.
WaveX
WaveX is a dedicated media-tech startup accelerator and
incubator launched by the MIB.
It supports startups working in AVGC-XR and other emerging media technologies. WaveX aims to help startups strengthen their technologies, develop market-ready solutions and explore global opportunities.
States Leading India's AVGC-XR Growth Story
Karnataka’s
AVGC-XR Policy 3.0 supports skill development, infrastructure, production grants and financial incentives for AVGC-XR companies. The state also operates the
KITVEN AVGC Fund
, with a ₹20-crore corpus to invest in companies working in AVGC and related sectors.
Maharashtra’s
AVGC-XR Policy 2025 has a financial plan of ₹3,268 crore and a vision extending to 2050. The policy provides a dedicated framework for expanding the state’s AVGC-XR ecosystem through government-backed support and infrastructure.
Telangana’s 2016 IMAGE Policy
established a dedicated framework for Animation, VFX, Gaming and Comics, anchored by Hyderabad’s IMAGE Tower. The ecosystem features 150+ AVGC/VFX companies, 140+ gaming and animation companies, 30,000 direct jobs and 100 startups onboarded through Software Technology Parks of India (STPI)-IMAGE, supported by production infrastructure, training and global cloud access.
Tamil Nadu’s
AVGC-XR Policy 2026 targets 200+ startups, around 2 lakh jobs and up to 20% of India’s AVGC-XR market by 2030. It also provides a support for the "ELCOT Viyan AVGC-XR Centre of Excellence” in Chennai as a hub and spokes at Coimbatore, Madurai, Tiruchirappalli, Salem and Tirunelveli regions over the next three years.
Kerala’s
AVGC-XR Policy 2024 focuses strongly on building a specialised talent pipeline. It proposes industry-aligned job roles, faculty development and AVGC-XR courses covering VR, AR, gaming, VFX and digital art, from schools through higher education. The mission aims to create
50,000 new jobs in the AVGC-XR industry, by 2029,
solidifying Kerala’s commitment to fostering a thriving knowledge-based economy.
Madhya Pradesh’s
AVGC-XR Policy 2025 combines Centres of Excellence, AVGC-XR labs and targeted skilling with investment incentives. The policy also supports capital investment, employment generation, production costs, quality certification and IP creation.
Uttar Pradesh
is developing an AVGC-XR Park in Jewar, near Noida International Airport and the proposed International Film City. The park will integrate animation, VFX, gaming, motion capture, virtual production and XR facilities. It aims to attract investment, support startups, create skilled employment and strengthen the state’s digital creative economy.
Rajasthan
announced its AVGC-XR Policy 2024 in the State Budget 2024-25 to strengthen the animation, VFX, gaming, comics and immersive technology ecosystem. The policy provides production incentives of
up to ₹50 lakh for eligible animation/VFX/AR/VR
projects and
₹1 crore
for
eligible game development.
Gujarat
is actively positioning itself as a key AVGC-XR hub through focused government initiatives. The state is in an advanced stage of preparing a comprehensive AVGC-XR policy supporting infrastructure, skilling, and startups. Moreover, the state already has a strong educational base - 16 institutions offering Animation, VFX and Gaming courses - providing a ready talent pipeline.
Way Forward
Immersive technologies represent more than a new entertainment medium. They are a strategic lever for India's creative economy, education system, and cultural preservation. As India strengthens its AVGC-XR ecosystem through coordinated national and state-level efforts, it is well-positioned to become a global hub for immersive content and innovation. This convergence of creativity and cutting-edge technology aligns closely with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, where a technologically empowered, self-reliant India leads in emerging sectors.

Catch the Rain Campaign at a Glance
Catch the Rain is a nationwide campaign focused on
rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge,
and
water-body restoration
. The campaign encourages communities and institutions to conserve rainwater and strengthen water security. It promotes cleaning of ponds and water reservoirs to maximise monsoon water retention. It also encourages
afforestation
to enhance green coverage in water-retention areas.
Key water conservation actions recommended during this campaign are:
Adopt rainwater harvesting systems in homes, societies and workplaces.
Install recharge pits and shafts at suitable locations.
Repair unused borewells to facilitate groundwater recharge.
Restore baolis, wells and traditional water bodies.
Desilt ponds and reservoirs to enhance water retention.
Promote tree plantation in water retention and recharge areas.
Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari (JSJB) 1.0
(2024)
Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari 1.0
strengthened community participation
in water conservation. JSJB 1.0 was implemented from 1 April 2024 to 31 May 2025. The initiative followed the principles of
Community, CSR, and Cost - the 3Cs
. It also mobilized
convergence with ongoing government schemes
to accelerate water conservation efforts. The initiative promoted
low-cost
groundwater recharge and water storage structures. It also supported the
revival
of defunct borewells and
locally appropriate
solutions. The structures were developed through a Whole-of-Government and Whole-of-Society approach. During this campaign, more than
10 lakh
groundwater recharge structures were constructed, with more than
27 lakh
artificial recharge structures reported.
Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari 2.0
(2025)
Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari 2.0, launched on 1 June 2025, built upon the earlier initiative. It focused particularly on groundwater recharge in
over-exploited and critical districts
. The approach emphasised
low-cost
and
hyper-local interventions
. In November 2025, exemplary contributions under JSJB 1.0 were recognised during the
6th National Water Awards
.
Impact Evaluation and Achievement of JSJB Initiative
Under the Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari (JSJB) initiative, over
1.55 crore Artificial Recharge and Storage Structures
have been constructed. Further, an Impact Evaluation Study of JSJB 1.0 was conducted, which evaluated
23 lakh structures
using rainfall data between 1 June 2025 and 31 December 2025. The study estimated that these interventions have resulted in
2.43 billion cubic metres of groundwater recharge
.
Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari: Catch the Rain (JSJB: CTR) (2026)
The 2026 initiative, launched on June 1,2026, expand
ed
the
JSJB
approach
by
integrat
ing it
with the Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain campaign
.
The campaign focused on rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge, water conservation, creation of water assets, and community participation. It promoted locally appropriate, low-cost interventions and strengthened
climate resilience
through sustainable water management.
The campaign leveraged
convergence across several government schemes
like VB-G RAM G, Per Drop More Crop under PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY), Repair, Renovation and Restoration of Water Bodies under PMKSY, CAMPA, Finance Commission Grants and other state government schemes.  The initiative brought together Panchayati Raj Institutions, urban local bodies, women’s groups, youth, educational institutions, civil society organisations and local communities. These stakeholders support
planning, implementation
and
community-led water conservation
.
JSJB: CTR portal
and
mobile application
have been instrumental in strengthening transparency, monitoring and facilitating public feedback.
Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain (JSA: CTR)
Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain was launched on
22 March
2021
on
World Water Day
. Its guiding theme was:
“Catch the Rain, Where It Falls, When It Falls.”
The campaign builds on the success of
Jal Shakti Abhiyan 2019
, which covered 1,592 water-stressed blocks across 256 districts for promoting rainwater harvesting. It also promoted groundwater recharge, watershed development, rejuvenation of water bodies, afforestation, and community participation through a
Jan Andolan
approach. The campaign has since been
implemented annually with evolving themes and focus areas
:
Year
Theme / Focus
Key Areas of Activity
2021
Catch the Rain, Where It Falls, When It Falls
Rainwater harvesting & water Conservation; Geo-tagging of water bodies; Scientific water conservation planning; Jal Shakti Kendras and awareness activities
2022
Expanding Water Conservation Activities
Restoration of traditional water bodies; Groundwater recharge and watershed development; Wetland and river rejuvenation; Spring-shed development and catchment protection
2023
Source Sustainability for Drinking Water
Focus on 150 water-stressed districts; Strengthening drinking water sources; Groundwater recharge and source sustainability; Field monitoring and community participation
2024
Nari Shakti se Jal Shakti
Women-led water conservation initiatives; Desilting and cleaning of water bodies; Revival of abandoned borewells for recharge; Afforestation and rejuvenation of local water resources
The 2024 campaign highlighted women-led water conservation initiatives.
Their contributions continue to be recognized through the
Swachh Sujal Shakti Samman
, celebrating exemplary efforts in water conservation, sanitation, and hygiene.
Jal Shakti Kendras
Jal Shakti Kendras (JSKs) serve as
district-level knowledge and facilitation hubs
. They support communities and local administrations through:
Providing information on water harvesting techniques
Providing technical guidance
Supporting water conservation planning and implementation
From Rainwater Harvesting to Rural Resilience
Water conservation has evolved into a community-driven movement focused on sustainable water management. Initiatives such as Catch the Rain and Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari promote rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge, and restoration of water bodies. Scientific planning, local ownership, and convergence of resources are strengthening water security, rural livelihoods, and climate resilience. By linking community ownership with convergence, digital oversight, and asset creation,
JSJB: CTR is laying the foundation for a water-secure Bharat
.
